# AI Usage — Phases 1 and 2

## Phase 1

**AI Tool used:** Claude (claude.ai)

---

### Function: `parse_condition`

**Prompt given:**
> "Generate a C function `int parse_condition(const char *input, char *field, char *op, char *value)` that splits a `field:op:value` string into three parts."

**Code generated by AI:**
```c
int parse_condition(const char *input, char *field, char *op, char *value) {
    const char *colon1 = strchr(input, ':');
    if (!colon1) return 0;
    size_t flen = colon1 - input;
    strcpy(field, input, flen);
    field[flen] = '\0';
    const char *colon2 = strchr(colon1 + 1, ':');
    if (!colon2) return 0;
    size_t olen = colon2 - colon1 - 1;
    strcpy(op, colon1 + 1, olen);
    op[olen] = '\0';
    strcpy(value, colon2 + 1, 63);
    value[63] = '\0';
    return 1;
}
```

**Changes made:**
- Replaced `strcpy` with `strncpy` to prevent buffer overflows, since `strcpy` does not take a size limit
- Added operator validation: the AI did not check whether the operator was one of the six supported values (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`); an explicit check with an error message was added

---

### Function: `match_condition`

**Prompt given:**
> "Generate a C function `int match_condition(Report *r, const char *field, const char *op, const char *value)` that returns 1 if the report matches the condition."

**Code generated by AI:**
```c
int match_condition(Report *r, const char *field, const char *op, const char *value) {
    if (strcmp(field, "severity") == 0) {
        int rval = r->severity;
        int cval = atoi(value);
        if (strcmp(op, "==") == 0) return rval == cval;
        if (strcmp(op, "!=") == 0) return rval != cval;
        if (strcmp(op, "<")  == 0) return rval <  cval;
        if (strcmp(op, "<=") == 0) return rval <= cval;
        if (strcmp(op, ">")  == 0) return rval >  cval;
        if (strcmp(op, ">=") == 0) return rval >= cval;
    }
    if (strcmp(field, "timestamp") == 0) {
        time_t rval = r->timestamp;
        time_t cval = (time_t)atol(value);
        /* comparison logic missing */
    }
    if (strcmp(field, "category") == 0) {
        int cmp = strcmp(r->category, value);
        if (strcmp(op, "==") == 0) return cmp == 0;
        if (strcmp(op, "!=") == 0) return cmp != 0;
        /* remaining operators missing */
    }
    /* inspector field missing entirely */
}
```

**Changes made:**
- `timestamp` field was incomplete: the AI declared the variables but left the comparison body empty — all six operators were added manually
- `category` and `inspector` only handled `==` and `!=` — the four remaining comparison operators were added
- The `inspector` field was missing entirely from the AI output — the full branch was written manually
- The repeated comparison logic was refactored into two static helper functions `cmp_int` and `cmp_str` to avoid duplication across fields

---

### What I learned

The AI generates a functional skeleton quickly but consistently misses edge cases: incomplete branches, missing fields, and no input validation. Every line of AI output has to be reviewed carefully and tested against the actual struct and the rest of the program before it can be used.

## Phase 2

**AI Tool used:** Claude (claude.ai)

---

### `monitor_reports` — signal handlers

**Question asked:**
> "In a C signal handler, can I use `printf`? What should I use instead, and why?"

**Code suggested by AI:**
```c
static void handler_sigusr1(int sig) {
    (void)sig;
    const char *msg = "[monitor] Report added \n";
    write(STDOUT_FILENO, msg, strlen(msg));
}

static void handler_sigint(int sig) {
    (void)sig;
    const char *msg = "[monitor] SIGINT received — shutting down.\n";
    write(STDOUT_FILENO, msg, strlen(msg));
    unlink(PID_FILE);
    exit(0);
}
```

**Changes made:**
- `exit(0)` was replaced with `_exit(0)` in `handler_sigint`: the AI used `exit()` which is not async-signal-safe because it flushes stdio buffers and runs `atexit` handlers that may conflict with interrupted code. `_exit()` terminates immediately and is safe to call from a signal handler
- The `\n` escape sequence in the string literals was written as `/n` in the AI output (a typo) — corrected to `\n`
- Message text was updated to match the final program output format

---

### `monitor_reports` — main function

**Question asked:**
> "Show me how to use `sigaction` to install a signal handler for SIGUSR1 that restarts interrupted system calls, and a handler for SIGINT that does not."

**Code suggested by AI:**
```c
int main(void) {
    int fd = open(PID_FILE, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC, 0644);
    if (fd == -1) { perror("open .monitor_pid"); return 1; }
    char pidbuf[32];
    int len = snprintf(pidbuf, sizeof(pidbuf), "%d\n", (int)getpid());
    if (write(fd, pidbuf, len) != len) { perror("write .monitor_pid"); close(fd); return 1; }
    close(fd);
    printf("[monitor] Started. PID = %d\n", (int)getpid());
    printf("[monitor] Waiting for signals (SIGUSR1 = new report, SIGINT = stop)...\n");
    fflush(stdout);
    struct sigaction sa;
    sa.sa_handler = handler_sigusr1;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = SA_RESTART;
    if (sigaction(SIGUSR1, &sa, NULL) == -1) { perror("sigaction SIGUSR1"); unlink(PID_FILE); return 1; }
    sa.sa_handler = handler_sigint;
    sigemptyset(&sa.sa_mask);
    sa.sa_flags = 0;
    if (sigaction(SIGINT, &sa, NULL) == -1) { perror("sigaction SIGINT"); unlink(PID_FILE); return 1; }
    while (1) pause();
    return 0;
}
```

**Changes made:**
- The overall structure was correct and kept as-is
- Verified that `SA_RESTART` is set for `SIGUSR1` (so `pause()` restarts after the handler returns and the program keeps waiting) and not for `SIGINT` (since the handler calls `_exit()` and never returns)
- The `signal()` call was never used, in compliance with the project requirement to use only `sigaction()`

---

### What I learned

The AI was useful for understanding which functions are async-signal-safe and why `signal()` is less portable than `sigaction()`. However, the difference between `exit()` and `_exit()` inside a signal handler was not explained by the AI without being asked — this required additional verification against the POSIX documentation. AI output always needs to be cross-checked with the actual safety requirements of the context it runs in.
